concept.name: Painting the tape
concept.definition: Engaging in a series of transactions — typically wash trades or matched orders — designed to create a false or misleading appearance of active trading or of price movement in a security, so that the publicly reported 'tape' attracts other investors. Section 9(a)(1)-(2) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 prohibits effecting such transactions for the purpose of inducing purchases or sales by others.
concept.intuition: You manufacture busy-looking trades and rising prints on the ticker so the crowd thinks something is happening and piles in — the activity is theater, not genuine demand.
concept.mechanics: Manipulators execute rapid, often self-referential or collusive trades at escalating prices in an otherwise thin stock. Because the consolidated tape reports every trade, the manufactured prints signal momentum to screeners and retail traders, into whose buying the manipulators sell.
concept.failure_modes: Genuine bursts of small-lot trading in illiquid names (e.g., around news) can look like tape painting in surveillance; the manipulative element is the fictitious or induced character of the activity and the purpose of deceiving observers.
concept.misconceptions: The term is often loosely applied to any suspicious price action at day-end; strictly it refers to creating a false appearance of trading activity, distinct from marking the close, which targets the settlement/closing price specifically.
concept.example: Two colluding accounts trade a penny stock back and forth 200 times in an hour at prices stepping from $0.50 to $0.80; the tape shows 'surging volume,' chatrooms notice, and the operators dump their real holdings into the arriving buyers.

citations.source: Securities Exchange Act of 1934, Section 9(a), 15 U.S.C. § 78i (U.S. Code, GPO)
